evals.prompt: I want to build the check-in system — the core interaction where Basil periodically asks the user how they're doing and they respond in free text. This is the thing that builds context over time.
evals.expected_output: A structured spec that treats the check-in as the primary interaction model, not a notification or logging reminder. Should probe: what triggers a check-in (scheduled? user-initiated? both?), what Basil does with the response, how responses feed into the memory/context layer, what the conversation flow looks like, and whether there are any PHI implications in free-text health journaling. Should NOT spec this as a 'logging reminder' or frame it around BG entry.

evals.prompt: Basil needs to remember things across conversations. Right now every chat session starts fresh. I want Basil to build up context about a user over time — like knowing they've been stressed at work, or that they always go low after exercise. How do we build that?
evals.expected_output: A spec for the persistent memory/context system. Should grapple with: what gets remembered vs forgotten, how memory is structured (not just chat logs), user transparency and control (view/delete memories), privacy implications, how memory informs future conversations, and technical dependencies (Supabase, the chat API). Should flag that this is foundational infrastructure, not a UI feature.

evals.prompt: What does onboarding look like? When someone opens Basil for the first time, how does the app establish that this is a companion, not just another T1D tracker? I want them to feel like they're meeting Basil, not setting up an app.
evals.expected_output: A spec focused on the emotional and relational framing of first-time experience, not just account setup steps. Should think about: how Basil introduces itself, what questions it asks to start building context, how to set expectations about what Basil is and isn't (especially the clinical boundary), how to differentiate from every other T1D app the user has seen. Should explicitly flag that onboarding is the first impression of the companion relationship.
